title: Community Day on the Open Ground

pages.text: It began with a poster on a wall: COMMUNITY DAY, Saturday, on the Open Ground, everyone welcome. The Assembly member, Madam Oduro, had asked the young people of five neighbourhoods to plan it together. Halima, Juliet, Theophilus, Awudu and Caleb met under a mango tree. “We each know our own streets,” said Halima. “Now we must learn each other’s.”

“Now we must learn each other’s.”

pages.text: On Saturday morning, the Open Ground filled with people in gloves and sashes. Boys from the lagoon settlement cleared the drain beside the ground. Girls from the zongo swept the path. Students from the estate brought sacks and tools, and the middle-income families brought water and snacks. Ramatu and Samuel handed out gloves. “Wear them properly,” said Awudu. “And nobody goes into the drain or the water. That is the rule.”

pages.alt: People in gloves and sashes sweep, carry sacks and clear a drain beside an open ground.

pages.text: Under a big canopy, nurses from the nearby clinic offered free screenings for blood pressure, eyesight and sugar levels. Theophilus’s mother was among them. A health officer explained the National Health Insurance Scheme and helped families to register or renew. “Every child has a right to health care,” she said, “and the scheme can cover many children’s medical costs.” A long queue formed, and nobody minded the wait.

pages.text: Juliet’s book corner was a hit. She had collected hundreds of storybooks from her estate and her school, and Samuel and Caleb were first in line. “Take as many as you can read,” she said, smiling. Richmond, the reader from the community school, read aloud to a circle of younger children. Samuel borrowed three. “I will return them,” he said, “and I will bring my friends.”

pages.text: At noon came the football friendly: Lagoon Side against a team from the estate. The estate boys had new boots, and the Lagoon Side boys had old ones, but nobody mentioned it. Caleb saved a penalty. Awudu scored from a free kick. The match ended in a draw, and both teams took the Fair Play trophy together. “Football is a language,” said Coach Hubert. “And today everyone speaks it.”

pages.text: Then came the speeches. Halima stood at the microphone, her note cards in her hand. “Nana, Reverend, Imam, Madam Assembly Member, distinguished ladies and gentlemen,” she began, and the crowd fell quiet. “We come from different streets, but we drink from the same tap, walk the same roads and breathe the same air. Rights belong to everyone, and so do duties. Let us build a community where no child is left behind.”

pages.text: When the sun began to sink, the Open Ground was clean, the drain was clear, and nobody wanted to leave. The elders sat together: the zongo chief, the imam, the pastor and the queen mother of the market. “This is what we need more of,” said the queen mother. Madam Oduro nodded. “Community Day will be held every term,” she announced. “And the young people will lead it.” A great cheer rose.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a speech begins with the correct address, such as “Mr Chairman, Reverend, Imam, distinguished ladies and gentlemen”. It states the topic, gives two or three clear points with examples, and ends with a call to action. It is written in polite, persuasive language, with no contractions or slang, and it is read aloud, so use short, strong sentences. Halima’s opening sentence names her audience and her purpose. The end.
